title: The persistent widow (Luke 18:1–8)
hookLine: a widow wears down an unjust judge simply by never stopping

cards: There's a judge in a certain city, and Jesus sums him up in one line: he doesn't fear God, and he doesn't care what anyone thinks. You can't appeal to his conscience, and you can't shame him.
And there's a widow in the same city, with no husband to speak for her and no money to smooth things along. Someone has wronged her, and she wants justice. She goes to the judge.
He says no. She comes back. He ignores her.
Every time the court sits, there she is. Finally the judge says to himself: I still don't fear God or care about anybody, but this woman is wearing me out. Give her what she wants.

teach.h: ALWAYS PRAY, AND NOT TO FAINT
teach.b: Luke gives the point before the story starts: Jesus told it to show "that men ought always to pray, and not to faint." Not to faint means not to lose heart.
And the thing to get right: the judge is not a picture of God. The story works by contrast.
If a crooked judge who cares about nobody finally gives in to someone who won't stop asking, how much more will God, who does care, hear the people who cry out day and night?
Jewish teachers had a name for this kind of argument: from the lesser to the greater. Now the funny part, hidden in the Greek.

teach.h: A BLACK EYE FOR THE JUDGE
teach.b: When the judge worries she'll weary him, Luke uses a word from the boxing ring: to hit under the eye, to give someone a black eye. He's half joking and half afraid.
A widow with no power at all, and the man who runs the court is worried about his face. Widows matter here.

Again and again the Hebrew Bible tells Israel to protect the widow, the orphan and the stranger, the people with no one to stand up for them. This widow has no one, so she stands up for herself, and doesn't stop.
The story ends with a question, not a bow: "when the Son of man cometh, shall he find faith on the earth?" As if the hard part isn't God listening. It's us still asking.

teach.h: KNOCK, AND IT SHALL BE OPENED.
teach.b: Matthew's Gospel has Jesus say it another way: "knock, and it shall be opened unto you."

how: Some Christians keep praying for the same person or need for months or years, sometimes on a written list, and churches often pray for the same people week after week until something changes.

games.why: she just keeps coming, and the man who fears nothing gives in, "lest by her continual coming she weary me."

practice: Bring back one thing you stopped asking for: a prayer you quit saying, a hope you set down long ago. Without arguing or trying to fix it, ask once more, to God if you pray, or honestly to yourself if you don't.
The widow didn't win on the first day; she just came back.

wordCard.voice: Widow. A woman with no husband to speak for her and no money to smooth things along, who wins by refusing to stop asking.

orig.note: Greek: to hit under the eye. the judge's word for what the widow might do to him.
